summary: Documents issues and potential problems raised against proposals that let one subnet span multiple links connected by routers. It lists the concerns for readers who might consider such a design. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some people wanted one neighborhood address to cover several streets with gates between them. This note lists the troubles that would cause.

subtitle: Why subnets should not span multiple network links

tldr.problem: Some network designs proposed allowing a single subnet to span multiple links connected by routers, similar to how airline hubs connect distant airports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents the fundamental problems this causes, including routing assumptions, multicast scope issues, and security risks.
tldr.outcome: The IPv6 working group rejected this design in favor of the traditional model where a subnet spans only a single link, though some protocols continued to use it.

today: RFC 4903 is an informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It documents the IAB consensus that the traditional model—a subnet spans one link—should be preserved. Most protocols and standards follow this model, though some legacy systems (such as Mobile IPv6 with home agents) continue to use multi-link subnets and must manage the implications.

sections.title: The History of Subnet Design
sections.content:
When networks were small, organizations could give each cable its own Internet address number. As networks grew, three options emerged: acquire separate numbers for each cable, treat all cables as one network (the transparent subnets approach), or divide a network number into smaller subnets assigned to each cable.

The IETF standardized the third approach with RFC 950, where routers and hosts learn a subnet mask that defines which part of an address identifies the network segment and which part identifies the host. This became the IPv4 model and was carried forward into IPv6. Since then, several working groups and external organizations have proposed allowing a subnet to span multiple links, bridged by routers—a concept the RFC examines to document why this fails.
sections.eli5: Long ago, networks were small. As they grew, people realized they needed to divide big networks into smaller pieces. The standard solution was to split addresses into network and segment parts, and that is still how networks work today. Some people wanted to break this rule and let one network segment span multiple physical connections.

sections.title: Core Concepts: Links, Subnets, and Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC clarifies two key concepts. A link is a topological area bounded by routers that decrement the TTL (Time To Live) field when forwarding packets. In contrast, a subnet uses the same address prefix and is—in the IPv4 and IPv6 models—associated with exactly one link. Multiple subnets can exist on a single link, but one subnet spans only one link.

This relationship between link and subnet is not accidental: it is the foundation for how hosts learn about neighbors, how multicast and broadcast reach only local devices, and how many security mechanisms assume a boundary at the link edge.
sections.eli5: A link is a piece of wire (or radio signal) where data travels without any router slowing it down. A subnet is an address range. The standard rule is one subnet per link. If you break that rule, everything that depends on the rule breaks too.

sections.title: TTL/Hop Limit and Application Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a critical problem: many applications and protocols embed assumptions about the relationship between a subnet and a link. Textbooks teach that a TTL of 1 confines packets to a subnet, and tools like traceroute rely on this. More importantly, protocols like Neighbor Discovery (ND) use TTL or Hop Limit values of 255 checked on receipt to ensure packets come from the local link.

When a subnet spans multiple links, routers decrement the TTL between those links, breaking packets with TTL=1 and preventing applications that expect TTL=255 to work across the subnet. The RFC cites Unix Network Programming, TCP/IP Illustrated, and vendor documentation—all teaching that TTL=1 means subnet-local delivery. Changing this assumption globally would break countless deployed systems.
sections.eli5: Programs learn from books that a TTL of 1 means the message stays in one neighborhood. If one neighborhood address spans two neighborhoods with a gate between them, the message dies at the gate. Programs expect this; breaking it breaks the programs.

sections.title: Multicast and Broadcast Limitations
sections.content:
Multicast and broadcast frames are only meant to reach devices on the same link—routers do not forward them. This is why multicast routing is separate from unicast routing and is not deployed everywhere. Many protocols rely on link-scoped multicast or broadcast for critical functions: routing protocols like OSPF and RIP, address management protocols like DHCP and Neighbor Discovery, and service discovery protocols like Bonjour and SSDP all use link-scoped multicast.

When a subnet spans multiple links, these packets cannot cross from one link to the other unless the router provides protocol-specific proxying. The RFC explains that adding proxies for the arbitrary number of existing protocols and future protocols does not scale and stifles innovation.
sections.eli5: Broadcast announcements only reach the people on your street because routers do not forward them. Many important systems rely on this—like how your mail carrier announces new addresses. If one address covers multiple streets, broadcasts cannot reach across, and proxies (people standing on the border re-announcing) would be needed. There are too many announcements to proxy them all.

sections.title: Recommended Link Models
sections.content:
The RFC recommends two models that avoid these issues. The multi-access link model allows multiple nodes on one link, including zero or more routers, with no TTL decrement between any nodes. The point-to-point link model has exactly two nodes and similarly avoids TTL decrement. Both preserve the principle that a subnet corresponds to a link.

A variant, the NBMA (Non-Broadcast Multi-Access) link model, eliminates multicast and broadcast entirely, which avoids the multicast routing problem but breaks any protocol relying on broadcast or multicast. The IAB recommends IETF working groups abandon multi-link subnet approaches and move to one of these models, or—for wide-area links like tunnels that need not support multicast across the full topology—accept the trade-offs of NBMA.
sections.eli5: The RFC suggests three ways to build networks that do not have these problems. Allow multiple computers on one wire with no gates (multi-access). Limit each connection to exactly two computers (point-to-point). Or permit no announcements at all (NBMA). All three work better than letting one address cover multiple wired connections with gates between them.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: Security protocols that assume a subnet boundary is also a link boundary will break. For example, Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) is defined only for single links and would not work across a multi-link subnet because link-layer addresses change at each hop. Some protocols mitigate spoofing attacks by requiring a TTL or Hop Limit of 255 on receipt, a check that assumes the sender is on the local link. If this restriction is removed or bypassed, off-link spoofing becomes easier and requires alternative defenses. This represents a shift in the security model that network operators must plan for.
sections.eli5: If one address covers multiple neighborhoods, security locks that worked before break. Locks that rely on checking that a message still has full TTL when it arrives stop working, because the message loses TTL crossing the internal gate.
